content: The evaluation of the fallopian tubes, commonly referred to as tubal patency testing, is a standard diagnostic procedure for women experiencing subfertility. This process typically involves flushing a contrast medium through the fallopian tubes and assessing their openness using imaging techniques such as radiographs, ultrasonography, or laparoscopy. Interestingly, many women have been observed to conceive within three to six months following tubal flushing, suggesting that this procedure might not only serve as a diagnostic tool but also as a potential treatment for infertility. However, there is ongoing debate regarding the type of contrast medium to use—oil-soluble contrast media (OSCM) or water-soluble contrast media (WSCM)—as this choice may influence pregnancy outcomes. A notable adverse event associated with tubal flushing is intravasation, where the contrast medium flows backward into the blood or lymphatic vessels. While this is typically asymptomatic, it carries a theoretical risk of embolism. The objective of this systematic review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of tubal flushing with OSCM and WSCM in improving fertility outcomes for women with subfertility. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing OSCM, WSCM, or no treatment. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering multiple databases and trial registries, with the most recent search conducted in April 2020. The quality of evidence was evaluated using GRADE methodology. Fifteen trials involving 3,864 women were included in the review. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations such as risk of bias, heterogeneity, and imprecision. 1. OSCM versus No Treatment: Four studies (506 women) compared tubal flushing with OSCM to no treatment. Tubal flushing with OSCM may increase the likelihood of live birth (odds ratio [OR] 3.27, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.57 to 6.85, low-quality evidence). This suggests that if the baseline chance of live birth without treatment is 11%, the chance with OSCM would range between 16% and 46%. Tubal flushing with OSCM may also increase the odds of clinical pregnancy (OR 3.54, 95% CI 2.08 to 6.02, low-quality evidence). If the baseline chance of clinical pregnancy without treatment is 9%, the chance with OSCM would range between 17% and 37%. No studies reported on adverse events such as intravasation, infection, hemorrhage, or congenital abnormalities. 2. WSCM versus No Treatment: One study (334 women) compared tubal flushing with WSCM to no treatment. The evidence is uncertain regarding whether WSCM increases live birth rates (OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.91, low-quality evidence). If the baseline chance of live birth without treatment is 21%, the chance with WSCM would range between 15% and 33%. Similarly, it is uncertain whether WSCM increases clinical pregnancy rates (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.84, low-quality evidence). If the baseline chance of clinical pregnancy without treatment is 27%, the chance with WSCM would range between 29% and 40%. One case of pelvic infection was reported in the WSCM group, while no infections were reported in the no-treatment group. Other adverse events, such as intravasation, hemorrhage, or congenital abnormalities, were not measured. 3. OSCM versus WSCM: Six studies (2,598 women) compared OSCM to WSCM. Three studies reported live birth outcomes, with two studies favoring OSCM (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.27 to 2.11; OR 3.45, 95% CI 1.97 to 6.03) and one study showing no significant difference (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.40). Due to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 86%), a meta-analysis was not performed. Tubal flushing with OSCM probably increases the odds of intravasation compared to WSCM (OR 5.00, 95% CI 2.25 to 11.12, moderate-quality evidence). If the baseline chance of intravasation with WSCM is 1%, the chance with OSCM would range between 2% and 9%. OSCM may increase the odds of clinical pregnancy compared to WSCM (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.85, low-quality evidence). If the baseline chance of clinical pregnancy with WSCM is 26%, the chance with OSCM would range between 28% and 39%. The evidence is uncertain regarding whether OSCM reduces the odds of infection (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.04 to 1.22, very low-quality evidence) or hemorrhage (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.06, very low-quality evidence). Three cases of congenital abnormalities were reported in the OSCM group, while none were reported in the WSCM group in one study (1,119 women). Due to the rarity of these events, no meta-analysis was performed. Conclusions: The evidence suggests that tubal flushing with OSCM may improve the chances of live birth and clinical pregnancy compared to no treatment, while the benefits of WSCM remain uncertain. When comparing OSCM to WSCM, OSCM may improve clinical pregnancy rates, but the evidence for live birth outcomes is inconclusive due to heterogeneity. OSCM is associated with a higher risk of asymptomatic intravasation. Adverse events, particularly long-term outcomes, are poorly reported across studies.
